texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: SUMMARY
texts.text: SUMMARY

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Vaccines generate long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells (Bmems) that may re-enter secondary germinal centers (GCs) to further mutate their B cell receptor upon boosting and re-exposure to antigen. We show in mouse models that lymph nodes draining the site of primary vaccination harbor a subset of Bmems that reside in the subcapsular niche, generate larger recall responses , and are more likely to re-enter GCs compared with circulating Bmems in non-draining lymph nodes. This location-dependent recall of Bmems into the GC in the draining lymph node was dependent on CD169 + subcapsular sinus macrophages (SSMs) in the subcapsular niche. In human participants, boosting of the BNT162b2 vaccine in the same arm generated more rapid secretion of broadly neutralizing antibodies, GC participation , and clonal expansion of SARS-CoV-2-specific B cells than boosting of the opposite arm. These data reveal an unappreciated role for primed draining lymph node SSMs in Bmem cell fate determination.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: INTRODUCTION
texts.text: INTRODUCTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Vaccines protect from recurrent infection and disease by inducing the secretion of neutralizing antibodies by long-lived plasma cells (PCs) 1 and by generating memory B cells (Bmems). 2 Long-lived PCs are terminally differentiated and can only secrete antibodies of fixed specificity and affinity for the original antigen. In contrast, Bmems have the potential to rapidly differentiate into short-lived PCs in subcapsular proliferative foci (SPF) 3 or re-enter secondary germinal centers (GCs) and further diversify their B cell receptor (BCR) to improve their affinity for the original antigen and broaden their specificity for antigenic variants. 4 The latter is critical for weakly cross-reactive Bmems to acquire higher affinity against rapidly mutating respiratory pathogens. 5 , 6 The PC vs. GC Bmem cell fate choice is therefore central to vaccination outcomes and the development of effective humoral immunity.

In contrast, Bmems have the potential to rapidly differentiate into short-lived PCs in subcapsular proliferative foci (SPF) 3 or re-enter secondary germinal centers (GCs) and further diversify their B cell receptor (BCR) to improve their affinity for the original antigen and broaden their specificity for antigenic variants. 4 The latter is critical for weakly cross-reactive Bmems to acquire higher affinity against rapidly mutating respiratory pathogens. 5 , 6 The PC vs. GC Bmem cell fate choice is therefore central to vaccination outcomes and the development of effective humoral immunity.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Bmems are heterogeneous in terms of their phenotype, 7 function, and anatomical location. 8 Studies in mice have shown that certain Bmems may preferentially differentiate into GC B cells or PCs, depending on whether they have undergone immunoglobulin class switch recombination from IgM to IgG 9 , 10 and whether they express the cell surface molecules CD80 and PD-L2 (CD273). 11 These data suggest that the different Bmem cell fates may be cell intrinsic and preprogrammed. However, these in vivo experiments were performed by isolating Bmems, typically from the spleen and lymph nodes (LNs) of immunized donors and adoptively transferring them into antigen-naive recipient mice. Critically, this approach overlooks the potential link between Bmem heterogeneity, anatomic location, and niche specialization. 8

texts.orig: More recently, investigators have performed more physiological in situ studies of recall responses by Bmems in their native tissue microenvironment. 3 , 12–14 Mesin, Schiepers et al. showed by precise cell fate mapping of antigen-specific B cells that secondary GCs are dominated by naive B cells and not by Bmems as originally thought. 13 Wong et al. have also showed that Bmems are more likely to differentiate into PCs than colonize secondary GCs. 15 This Bmem resistance to re-enter secondary GCs may explain the doctrine of original antigenic sin, or immune imprinting, whereby the antibody response against the original strain of a virus prejudices the subsequent response against a closely related but different strain of the virus. 16–18 In contrast, Kuraoka et al. showed that local boosting of the draining LN (dLN) on the same side as the original primary vaccine was more likely to recruit highly mutated, high-affinity Bmems into secondary GCs than distal boosting of the non-dLN (ndLN) on the opposite side. 14 The anatomical and niche-specific factors involved in these Bmem cell fate choices remain to be elucidated.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In addition to Bmems, memory T follicular helper (mTfh) cells have been shown to be enriched in the dLN. 12 , 19 , 20 Antigen drains from the skin to the skin-dLN via the afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus (SCS). We have previously shown that both Bmems 3 and mTfh 12 cells localize to the outer B cell follicle, where they scan CD169 + subcapsular sinus macrophages (SSMs) for antigen. These migratory behaviors suggested that cells residing in the subcapsular region, such as SSMs, lymphatic endothelial cells, 21 and marginal reticular cells, 22 may provide a niche for Bmems and Tfh cells, possibly through the provision of adhesion molecules, chemokines, cytokines, and survival factors. 23 B cells and SSMs in the subcapsular niche are interdependent. SSMs sample and capture antigen from the lymph to present intact to activate naive B cells 24–26 and Bmems. 3 In turn, SSMs depend on lymphotoxin-α1β2 provided by naive B cells for their maturation and functional specialization as poorly phagocytic antigen-presenting cells for B cells. 27 , 28

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Here, we tracked the migratory behavior and cell fate of Bmems in response to prime-boost vaccination with a model protein antigen. Our data show that murine Bmems in the dLN reside in the subcapsular niche where they interact with SSMs, in contrast to ndLN Bmems, which are located deeper in the follicle. The quality and quantity of the recall response to homologous immunogen was significantly higher when boosted in the ipsilateral dLN compared with the contralateral ndLN. These site-specific differences in the Bmem recall response were dependent on SSMs in the subcapsular niche. Analysis of boosted ndLNs that had been ' 'primed' ' with a non-cognate an- tigen showed that the ability of primed SSMs to support recall responses was agnostic of the immunogen. Finally, we show that SARS-CoV-2-naive healthy adult volunteers boosted with the second dose of the BNT162b2 on the same arm as the priming dose make superior early recall broadly neutralizing antibody (bNAb) responses when compared with volunteers boosted on the opposite arm. Taken together, these data show that primed SSMs control the quantity and quality of the Bmem recall response in the dLN and provide a rationale for administering the second dose of prime-boost vaccines in the same arm.

texts.orig: Location-dependent positioning of Bmems in the subcapsular niche
texts.text: Location-dependent positioning of Bmems in the subcapsular niche

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We first examined the in situ positioning of resting Bmems in the dLN and ndLN using the SWHEL mouse model to track B cell responses to hen-egg lysozyme (HEL) 29 , 30 (Figure S1A). This system generates long-lived immunoglobulin isotype-switched B220 + CD38 + CCR6 + Bmems that are enriched in the dLN compared with the ndLN (Figures S1B–S1D). Whole-mount imaging by two-photon microscopy revealed that more Bmems in the dLN localized within the SSM layer compared with those in the ndLN (Figures 1A–1C; Video S1). There were two times more Bmems inside the SSM layer in the dLN compared with Bmems in the ndLN. Conversely, there were more Bmems outside the SSM layer in the ndLN compared with the dLN (Figure 1D).

Whole-mount imaging by two-photon microscopy revealed that more Bmems in the dLN localized within the SSM layer compared with those in the ndLN (Figures 1A–1C; Video S1). texts.label: text
texts.orig: We next labeled SSMs in vivo with anti-CD169 and follicular stroma cells with anti-CD157 monoclonal antibody (mAb) 12 to enable visualization of Bmem antigen surveillance and patrolling behavior (Figures 1E and 1F; Video S2). Consistent with previous studies, 3 Bmems in the dLN were confined to the superficial follicle, and although they often crossed in and out of the subcapsular niche, they only made occasional incursions deeper into the follicle (Figures 1E and 1F; Video S2). In contrast, Bmems in the ndLN exhibited two distinct migration patterns (Figures 1E and 1F; Video S2). Some ndLN Bmems were confined to the subcapsular niche and scanned SSMs and a separate subpopulation was confined to the center of the follicle where they appeared to scan follicular dendritic cells (FDCs) for antigen. 31 Cell tracking showed that dLN Bmems spent more time in the SSM layer than ndLN Bmems (Figure 1G). Accordingly, they exhibited a more restricted migration pattern with a higher confinement index (Figure 1H). The motility of dLN Bmems was faster, with a median average speed of 7.4 μm/min compared with 4.2 μm/min for ndLN Bmems (Figure 1I). Accordingly, dLN Bmems were more superdiffusive than ndLN Bmems (Figure 1J). Thus, the anatomical location (dLN vs. ndLN) determines the position and scanning behavior by which Bmems interact with SSMs in search of antigen.

In the absence of SSMs, the positioning of Bmems in the dLN was similar to that in the ndLN. CSF1R blockade did not impact the positioning of ndLN Bmems (Figures 2B and 2D).

texts.orig: CSF1R blockade significantly altered the cellular dynamics of dLN Bmems (Figures 2E–2I; Video S3). In the absence of SSMs, we used the second harmonic generation (SHG) from collagen in the LN capsule as a proxy for the SSM layer (Figure 2E). SSM depletion changed the migration pattern of dLN Bmems (Figure 2F), and the median time spent in proximity to the capsule decreased (Figure 2G; Video S3). These data show that CSF1Rdependent SSMs are responsible for attracting and maintaining Bmems in the subcapsular niche in the dLN.

texts.orig: We next reactivated Bmems in situ by homologous boosting on the ipsilateral (dLN) or contralateral (ndLN) side with HEL conjugated to ovalbumin (OVA)-derived peptide (Figure 3A). Consistent with previous studies, 3 booster immunization of the dLN generated large clusters of reactivated Bmems on day 5 that were confined to the secondary GCs and SPF (Figures 3B and 3C; Video S4). In contrast, boosting of the ndLN generated large clusters of reactivated Bmems that were confined predominantly to the SPF, with only a few secondary GCs observed (Figures 3B and 3C; Video S4). Tiled mosaic images confirmed that boosting of the dLN preferentially gave rise to more GCs in secondary follicles in the cortex, whereas boosting of the ndLN preferentially gave rise to more Blimp-1 GFP + PCs in medullary cords (Figures S3A and S3B).

texts.orig: Mice were boosted 5 weeks after priming and the differences in the dLN and ndLN output quantified (Figures 3D–3F). In absolute terms, there was a 2.8-fold higher expansion of donorderived antigen-specific (HEL + ) B cells in the boosted dLN compared with the boosted ndLN (Figure 3E). This was associated with a 10-fold increase in donor-derived antigen-specific GC B cells (Figure 3E). There was no significant difference in the number of PCs (Figure 3E). In relative terms, the percentage of GC B cells was higher in the boosted dLN (Figure 3F) and the percentage of PCs higher in boosted ndLN (Figure 3F). We also boosted at 15 weeks after priming and observed similar prefer- ence for GC re-entry in the dLN compared with ndLN, although the differences were less marked than at 5 weeks (Figures 3G and 3H). The total number of reactivated B cells was higher at 15 compared with 5 weeks, possibly due to less antibody feedback. 34 Analysis of multiple time points confirmed that the secondary GC response peaks in the first week and that differences in the HEL-OVA recall response were not due to differences in cellular kinetics (Figure S3C). These data suggest that boosting the dLN provides larger recall responses and more GC re-entry than the ndLN.

texts.orig: The HyHEL10 BCR has very high affinity for wild-type HEL (K a = 2 × 10 10 M − 1 ). 35 We next used mutated HEL 3X in which three amino acid substitutions have been introduced to lower the affinity of the immunogen by 3-logs (K a = 1.2 × 10 7 M − 1 ) 36 to model GC affinity maturation. 37 As expected, more dLN Bmems had undergone affinity maturation to acquire HEL 3X binding than ndLN Bmems (Figure 3I). The dLN Bmem preference for GC differentiation was evident in both the high-affinity (HEL 3X high ) (Figure 3J) and low-affinity (HEL 3X low ) compartments (Figure 3K). Notably, there was more high-affinity PC in boosted dLN than ndLN. Consistent with this, there was no difference in the serum anti-HEL antibody IgG1 response to prime-boost vaccination with high-affinity wild-type HEL-OVA (Figure 3L). However, there was significantly greater secretion of affinity-matured total and IgG1 anti-HEL 3X in response to vaccination with HEL 3X -OVA with dLN vs. ndLN boosting (Figure 3M). We also observed larger recall responses, with more GC B cells and PCs in the boosted dLN compared with ndLN, but not in the percentage of GC B cells, in the endogenous recall polyclonal (non-transgenic) antibody response to R-phycoerythrin (PE) (Figure S3E). Taken together, these data show that the Bmem recall to immunogens is dependent on the site of vaccine boosting.

texts.orig: We next short-circuited T cell-B cell interactions by administration of an anti-CD40L blocking mAb to abort any persistent primary GCs in the dLN (Figure S3G). Antigen recall generated the same response pattern in anti-CD40L mAb compared with isotype-control-treated mice (Figure S3H). The anti-CD40L mAb did not alter the preference for GC differentiation in the boosted dLN in absolute numbers (Figure S3H) or relative terms (Figure S3I). Thus, the different Bmem recall responses in our system are not due to the boosting of persistent GCs in the dLN.

texts.text: Role of mTfh cells in niche-dependent control of Bmem cell fate

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To determine the role of antigen-specific mTfh cells, we used a system in which we switched the source of T cell help prior to boosting (Figure 4A). HEL-specific Bmems and OVA-specific mTfh cells were generated by adoptive transfer of SWHEL B cells and OT-II T cells followed by immunization with HEL-OVA. Naive Smarta T cells specific for the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) gp61-80 peptide were adoptively transferred before mice were boosted either with HEL-gp61 to activate SWHEL Bmems and naive Smarta T cells or with HEL-OVA to activate SW HEL Bmems and OT-II mTfh cells. This showed that switching the source of T cell help led to a reduction in the size of the total Bmem recall response, GC B cell, and PCs in both the boosted dLN and boosted ndLN (Figures 4B and 4C). These data indicate that T cell help provided by mTfh cells contributes to the overall size of the recall response in both the dLN and ndLN.

texts.orig: We next treated recipient mice with anti-CSF1R mAb or isotype control before boosting (Figure 4D). CSF1R blockade specifically led to an ∼80-fold reduction in the total number of donor-derived HEL + B cells in the boosted dLN but not in the ndLN (Figures 4E and 4F). This is a log-order of magnitude larger than the effect of switching T cell help from mTfh to naive T cells (Figure 4C). The impact of SSM depletion was most pronounced in the GC compartment, where there was a 90-fold decrease in the absolute number of dLN GC B cells (Figure 4F). In contrast, there was no statistically significant reduction in GC B cells in the boosted ndLN (Figure 4F). There was also a 30-fold decrease in the number of PCs in the boosted dLN and 5.6-fold reduction in the boosted ndLN (Figure 4F). These data indicate thatSSMs in the dLN control both the proliferative expansion and cell fate choices of Bmems.

texts.orig: Bmems in the dLN and ndLN are transcriptionally distinct
texts.text: Bmems in the dLN and ndLN are transcriptionally distinct

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We isolated Bmems from the dLN, ndLN, and spleen and naive SW HEL B cells from the LN and spleen that had been adoptively transferred, but not immunized, and performed single-cell transcriptomic profiling (Figures 5A, S4A, and S4B). Single-cell gene expression was visualized and annotated according to their transcriptional cell state and tissue of origin (Figure 5A). The three cell clusters corresponded largely to naive B cells in the LN and spleen (cluster 0), resident Bmems in the dLN (cluster 1), and recirculating Bmems in the ndLN and spleen (cluster 2) (Figure 5B). Donor-derived antigen-specific B cells from immunized dLN, ndLN, and spleen downregulated genes associated with the naive B cell state, including Vpreb3 , Bach2 , Fcer2a , Ighd , and Ighm , and upregulated the Bmem-associated genes Ccr6 , Cxcr3 , Cd44 , Apoe , Cd81 , Cd83 , and Il9r (Figure 5C). Interestingly, whereas dLN and ndLN Bmems expressed Ighg1 or Ighg2b , splenic Bmems expressed Ighm or Ighg3 heavy-chain genes (Figure 5C). Importantly, we did not detect the expression of genes associated with GC B cell differentiation, such as Aicda , S1pr2 , and Mki67 , in these cells, confirming the resolution of the primary GC response and their identity as bona fide Bmems.

texts.orig: Bmems across the three tissue compartments shared a common gene transcription module (module 7, n = 197 genes) that includes Marcks , Cd72 , Cd40 , Nfkbia , Aim2 , Cd180 , and Mzb1 (Figures 5D and 5E; Table S2). Genes uniquely upregulated in dLN Bmems (module 1, n = 173) included genes involved in lymphocyte adhesion, migration, and localization (Pik3cg , Runx3 , Icam1 , Vasp , and Lta) and BCR activation and GC formation (Prmt1 , Ep300 , Gimap4 , Ski , Cr2 , Dock8 , and Tbl1xr1; Figures 5E, 5F, and S4C; Table S1). Notably, Lta , which encodes lymphotoxin-α , is important for the differentiation and maintenance of SSMs. 27 , 38 Genes uniquely upregulated in ndLN Bmems (module 3, n = 451) and upregulated in ndLN and splenic Bmems (module 4, n = 476) included genes associated with cell migration, motility, and LN tissue residence (Klf2 , Cd69 , Rgs2 , Gpr183 , S1pr3 , and Cxcr4), B cell activation (Cd69 , Tlr7 , and Cd83) and regulation of PC vs. GC B cell differentiation (Egr1 , Nfkbid , Bhlhe40 , Cd83, Cxcr4 , and Foxp1; Figures 5E, 5F, and S4C; Table S1). Downregulation of Klf2 , which encodes Kru¨ ¨ ppel-like factor 2, and its transcriptional target S1pr1 , is required for the tissue residence of CD8 + memory T cells and prevents their recirculation. 39 To test whether the downregulation of Klf2 (Figures 5F and S4C) contributed to the superior recallability of dLN Bmems, we used the 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl conenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitor lovastatin to induce Klf2 expression 40 (Figure S4D). Lovastatin treatment specifically impacted on the recall response in dLN but not ndLN, with impaired GC and PC differentiation (Figure S4E). These data indicate that dLN and ndLN harbor transcriptionally distinct Bmem subsets.

texts.orig: We next performed ligand-receptor pair analysis using NicheNet. 41 This analysis predicted that ligands expressed on the surface of SSMs were likely contributors to differential gene expression in dLN Bmems in contrast to ndLN Bmems, indicated by theirregulatory potential scores between ligands and downstream differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Figure 5G). For example, NicheNet identified potential interactions between prioritized ligand genes expressed bySSMs, such as the macrophage migration inhibition factor gene (Mif), andpredicted receptors expressed by dLN Bmems, such as Cd74 , Cd44 , and Cxcr4 (Figure 5G). This interaction was associated with the upregulated expression of genes in the Mif gene regulatory network (regulon), such as Dhx30 , Tnf, f, Ccnd2 , Cd44 , Cd164 , and Cpeb2 (Figure 5H). Other notable potential interactions include cell adhesion between SSM-expressed Itgam and Itgb2 , encoding the proteins CD11b and CD18, respectively, with Icam1 expressed by dLN Bmems, which are predicted to control the expression of Ighg2b and Tnf (Figure 5H). Thus, SSM-Bmem interactions in the dLN map to a niche-dependent regulon with Cxcr3-Ccl5 , Cd44-Mif, f, and Icam1-Itgam/Itgb2 as central regulators of Cd44 , Tnf, f, Dhx30 , Ccdn2 , Cd164 , Cpeb2 , Cxcr3 , and Ighg2b gene expression (Figure 5H). Conversely, the regulatory interactions predicted between SSMs and ndLN Bmems yielded diminished regulatory potentials, suggesting a reduced explanatory power of SSM-derived signaling for the gene expression by ndLN in comparison with dLN Bmems (Figure 5H). For example, SSM-expressed Cxcl10 was predicted to interact with ndLN Bmem-expressed Cxcr3 , Dpp4 , and Sdc4 (Figure 5H). These analyses are consistent with the imag- ingdata thatBmem-SSMinteractions are more frequentin thedLN than the ndLN.

texts.orig: We hypothesized that the initial exposure to vaccine may have primed the dLN SSMs in readiness for subsequent antigen encounter. To test this, we set up a response in which the ' 'dLN' ' was primed with the cognate antigen HEL-OVA and the ' 'ndLN' ' was primed with the irrelevant antigen PE or control (Figure 6A). Analysis of the recall response showed that priming of the ndLN with an irrelevant antigen significantly increased the total number of responding cells and this was specific to the GC compartment (Figure 6B). This was associated with an increase in the percentage of GC B cells and decrease in the percentages of PCs (Figure 6C). We depleted SSMs with the anti-CSF1R mAb and this abolished the enhanced ndLN recall response to HEL-OVA from prior priming withPE (Figures 6Band 6C). Thus, synchronous priming of the ndLN with an irrelevant antigen primes the SSMs and converts the recall response to resemble that of the dLN.

texts.orig: To test the impact of boosting location in human subjects, we recruited 30 healthy volunteers who were SARS-CoV-2-naive and performed a clinical study of boosting the homologous BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine, which encodes the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, either in the same (boosted dLN, n = 20) or opposite arm (boosted ndLN, n = 10) 3 weeks after the priming dose (Figure 7A; Table S3). The groups did not differ in terms of age (boosted dLN median age 38 years vs. boosted ndLN median age 43 years; p = 0.065) or gender (boosted dLN 40% male vs. boosted ndLN 45% male; p = 0.79) (Table S3). Fine needle biopsy (FNB) of both axillary LNs 42 was performed in a subset of 18 participants (n = 9, boosted dLN; n = 9, boosted ndLN) on days 5–7 after the second (booster) vaccine dose

texts.orig: ELISA of the serum showed that the total anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG antibody recall response was short-lived, peaked at the days 5–7 time point, and waned thereafter in the dLN participants (Figure 7D). In contrast, the response was delayed in the ndLN participants and peaked at the 4-week time point. These data are consistent with previous studies showing that the BNT162b2 antibody response is relatively short-lived. 46–49 Notably, at the days 5–7 time point after boosting, there were significantly higher serum antibody levels in the boosted dLN than boosted ndLN (Figure 7D). This was confirmed by a livecell-based flow cytometric assay (Figure S6B). 50 , 51 Analysis of the quality of the neutralizing antibody (NAb) response 52–54 showed that, at days 5–7, dLN participants had significantly higher levels of serum NAbs against the ancestral strain (Figure 7E). Critically, dLN boosting generated superior early NAb against SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern Delta (Figure 7F), Omicron BA.1, Omicron BA.2, and Omicron BA.5 (Figure 7G). The differences were not present prior to the second dose and serum NAbs were not significantly different at the 4-week and 4- to 6-month time points. These data suggest a more rapid secondary GC response and enhanced affinity maturation.

texts.orig: We performed single-cell transcriptomic analysis of 24,211 B cells from the FNB samples on days 5–7 post boosting from a subgroup of six participants (boosted dLN n = 3; boosted ndLN n = 3) and identified 7 clusters of cells (Figures 7J, S6C, and S6D; Table S4) based on the relative expression of naive B cell genes (HVCN1 , CCR7 , IL4R , TCL1A , IGHD , and IGHM), Bmem (FCRL5 , FCRL4 , CR2 , GPR183 , KLF2 , CD24 , CD27 , and TNFRSF13B), GC B cell genes (BACH2 , SERF2 , ELL3 , MKI67 , SERPINA9 , MME , RGS13 , and BCL6), and PC genes (HSP90B1 , PRDM1 , FKBP11 , SEC11C , XBP1 , JCHAIN , IRF4 , CD38 , IGHG1 , and IGHA1). This analysis confirmed the greater expansion of GC B cells in the boosted dLN compared with the boosted ndLN (Figure 7K). Analysis of the BCR repertoire also revealed greater clonal diversity of GC B cells and PCs (Figure 7L), suggesting that boosting the same arm maintains a broader B cell repertoire. We further analyzed the BCR sequences from 71 B cells, associated with 30 clones, which mapped to previously reported SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies or BCRs. This revealed that there were more expanded vaccineinduced B cell clones in the boosted dLN than the boosted ndLN (Figure 7M). The SARS-CoV-2-specific immunoglobulin heavy and kappa light chain gene (IGH-IGK) clones appeared to have accumulated more immunoglobulin heavy chain variable region gene (IGHV) somatic hypermutations (SHMs), although this was not statistically significant (Figure S6E). Taken together, these data indicate that boosting of vaccine responses in the same arm as the priming dose generates superior depth and breadth of recall responses in the first week.

texts.orig: DISCUSSION
texts.text: DISCUSSION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Respiratory pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2 pose a major challenge to vaccination success due to their ability to adapt and escape from vaccine-induced host immunity. 55 This is particularly problematic, as the host response to the original immunogen may lock in future responses and be ineffective against closely related strains of the virus. 16–18 Here, we investigated the cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to this immune imprinting and identify a critical site-specific role for SSMs in the dLN subcapsular niche in regulating the quality and quantity of Bmem responses to recall antigen.

texts.orig: The protective role of serum containing antibodies against diphtheria and tetanus was first demonstrated in 1890 by von Behring and Kitasato. 56 Gowans and Uhr subsequently showed that immunological memory could be adoptively transferred by small thoracic duct lymphocytes 57 that include recirculating Bmems. Thus, serum antibodies provide a passive first layer and Bmems provide an active second layer of immunity against reinfection. 58 Bmems are transcriptionally distinct from naive B cells 59 and are heterogeneous in terms of their origin, function, and fate. 58 In addition to circulating Bmems in the blood, tissue-resident Bmems also occupy and patrol multiple different anatomical compartments, including non-lymphoid tissues such as the lung. 60–63 There is emerging evidence that their cell fate potential is linked to their anatomic location in the body. 8 However, with regard to secondary lymphoid tissue, the distinction between Bmems in the dLN and ndLN was only recently appreciated with the move by the field away from the adoptive Bmem cell transfer systems pioneered in the 1960s by Gowans to the more physiological in situ models of Bmem recall. 2 , 8 These in situ models mimic the natural state in which humans are vaccinated and allow for holistic assessment of recall responses that include the contribution of Bmem-extrinsic factors such as antigen-presenting SSMs, 3 stromal cell niches, 23 mTfh cells, 12 and antibody feedback mechanisms. 34 , 64 , 65

texts.orig: We showed that Bmems residing in the dLN are pre-positioned in the subcapsular niche, where they are ideally placed to interact with SSMs that directly capture and present antigen from the afferent lymphatic vessels that drain into the SCS. 3 , 24–26 The migration pattern of dLN Bmems shows that they are confined to the subcapsular region and rarely venture deeper into the follicle. This search strategy optimizes the probability of their encounter with antigen the moment it arrives in the SCS. In contrast, ndLN Bmems are localized both in the subcapsular region and also deeper in the follicle. Their behavior is reminiscent of circulating naive B cells that enter the LN via high endothelial venules (HEVs) and scan, in addition to SSMs, 25 FDCs in the center of the follicle that trap antigen-containing immune complexes. 31 This search strategy allows for the possibility that antigen had drained earlier to the LN and been transported into the follicle. 27 These differences in cell migration are matched by differences in transcriptional cell states, consistent with dLN and ndLN Bmems being distinct cell subsets. Bmems in the dLN upregulated cell adhesion molecules such as Icam1 , which would facilitate their cellular interactions with SSMs via Itgam/Itgb2 (CD11b/CD18). Bmems in ndLN displayed similar gene expression profiles to Bmems in the spleen, consistent with their recirculating pattern. This includes the expression of genes involved in cell trafficking, such as Klf2 , 66 Cd69 , 67 and Gpr183 . 68

texts.orig: We showed that CSF1R blockade depleted SSMs but not dLN Bmems, indicating that they were dispensable for Bmem survival. In the absence of SSMs, dLN Bmems relocated deeper into the follicle and adopted migratory behaviors similar to those of ndLN Bmems. Thus, SSMs are critical for maintaining Bmem positioning in the dLN subcapsular niche but are not required for their cell survival. Bmems, in turn, express Lta and, like naive B cells, are able to provide the lymphotoxin signals needed for SSM maturation and maintenance. 27 , 38 The mutualism between SSMs and Bmems underscores the importance of the subcapsular niche for local immune memory. We performed ligand-receptor pair analysis to explore the SSM-Bmem interaction potentials and identified a niche-dependent regulon controlled by receptor-ligand interactions between Cxcr3-Ccl5 , Cd44-Mif, f, and Icam1-Itgam/Itgb2 . We propose that this regulon may contribute to their localization and cell differentiation potentials. However, the dLN recall response was not impacted when we blocked CXCR3 or ICAM-1, possibly due to redundancies between these and other pathways. The single-cell transcriptomic analysis also showed upregulation of genes that favor GC differentiation in the dLN (such as Prmt1 69 , 70 ) and genes that repress GC formation (such as Bhlhe40 67 ) and favor PC differentiation (such as Egr1 71 ) in the ndLN. Thus, location-dependent cell-intrinsic molecular programs also contribute to the differential recall responses.

texts.orig: recall. The importance of SSMs in regulating dLN Bmem recall was shown by CSF1R blockade. In addition to Bmems, mTfh cells also reside in the subcapsular niche, 12 and the critical role of Tfh cells in controlling the primary GC response is well recognized. 72 In our in situ model, mTfh cells also control the size of the Bmem proliferative expansion, but this was an order of magnitude less than the contribution of SSMs. Importantly, mTfh cells did not contribute to the preferential GC re-entry of dLN compared with ndLN Bmems. The critical role of SSMs suggested that antigen exposure may have primed them to better retain and reactivate Bmems in the dLN subcapsular niche. We showed by synchronously immunizing the ndLN with an irrelevant antigen that we were able to increase GC re-entry and convert ndLN recall response to resemble the dLN. CSF1R blockade abolished this effect indicating that it was dependent on SSMs. Thus, SSMs primed by the initial antigen encounter are able to promote Bmem GC re-entry in recall response to a different antigen. It will be interesting in future studies to determine the signals involved in their generation and the molecular differences between ' 'naive' ' and ' 'primed' ' SSMs.

texts.orig: The PC vs. GC cell fate choice is largely thought to be governed by the strength of the BCR signal and the quality of T cell help provided by mTfh cells. We showed here that the site of antigen recall can also influence the cell fate choice, providing an additional layer of control. The magnitude of the in situ monospecific recall response to HEL was significantly larger in the dLN compared with the ndLN. The quality of the response was also significantly better in the dLN, especially for low-affinity antigens, leading to increased secretion of affinitymatured antibodies. These differences were most marked in response to boosting with the low-affinity antigen HEL 3X -OVA. Importantly, they were also evident in the recall response to the polyclonal antigen by wild-type B cells. This preferential reentry of dLN compared with ndLN Bmems into secondary GCs is consistent with observations by Kuraoka et al., who distinguished between ' 'local' ' boosting of dLN and ' 'distal' ' boosting of ndLN. 14 It is also consistent with the study by Mesin, Schiepers et al., who also showed that boosting of dLN generated twice as many fate-mapped Bmem-derived GCs as the ndLN. 13 The data presented here pinpoint the cellular and molecular interactions between SSMs and Bmems in the dLN subcapsular niche as the key driver of this superior dLN Bmem Our mouse data predict that serial vaccination in the same arm would activate a subset of dLN-resident Bmems to re-enter secondary GCs and diversify their antibody response to crossneutralize antigenic variants. The advent of the COVID-19 global pandemic with exposure to the novel pathogen SARS-CoV-2 allowed us to test this in a clinical study that compared giving the second (booster) dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine ipsilateral or contralateral to the first (priming) dose to SARS-CoV-2naive individuals. There are important differences between our murine studies, which examined a monoclonal B cell response to a protein antigen, and the human studies, which examined a polyclonal B cell response to an mRNA-encoded antigen. Notably, in our mouse models there are no persistent GCs in the dLN, whereas persistent GCs are a feature of mRNA vaccination. 43 Despite these differences, we showed that ipsilateral boosting of the dLN generated superior early SARS-CoV-2spike-specific NAb levels against the ancestral, Delta, Omicron BA.1, Omicron BA.2, and Omicron BA.5 variants. This NAb response was associated with increased GC participation and SHM in the responding B cells and corroborates the mouse data, which showed more rapid mobilization of dLN Bmems into the secondary GC compared with the ndLN. The BNT162b2 vaccine has been shown to induce serum NAbs

texts.orig: with a half-life of only 56–66 days. 73 Interestingly, a recent systematic review and meta-analysis has shown that the vaccine efficacy against SARS-CoV-2 also wanes, with a half-life of 87 days for Omicron. 74 These data are consistent with the results of our vaccine study, which showed similar waning of the antibody response by 6 months. Mathematical modeling supports the more rapid growth rate and earlier peak of NAbs from ipsilateral dLN boosting. Importantly, these differences are predicted to provide significantly greater vaccine efficacy against ancestral, Delta, and Omicron BA.1 at 1-week post vaccination. We were unable to model the kinetics of NAbs to the Omicron BA.2 and BA.5 variants because many of the results were below the limit of detection. This rapid generation of a high-quality bNAb recall response may be critical in a pandemic to rapidly generate herd immunity.

texts.orig: These data are also consistent with an observational study of 301 individuals who received the BNT162b2 vaccine, which showed that the median NAb titer at 13–15 days was slightly higher in the ipsilateral compared with the contralateral boosted group. 75 This study did not test for broadly neutralizing ability to variants of concern nor did they perform FNB of the LN or singlecell analysis of the BCR repertoire for SHM. The small difference observed in NAb titers may relate to the single later time point of 2 weeks in this study; in contrast, we observed substantial differences in both quantity and quality of the bNAb response earlier on days 5–7. Longitudinal analysis of serum samples in our clinical study showed that the benefits of ipsilateral boosting of the dLN had waned by 4 weeks and was negligible at 4–6 months. Importantly, real-world data from a retrospective analysis of 2,678,226 individuals vaccinated with BNT162b2 vaccine showed that 88.41% of individuals had ipsilateral boosting of the dLN and the rest had contralateral boosting of the ndLN. 76 Short-term effectiveness was greater for dLN than ndLN boosting, with less-frequent positive reverse-transcription PCR (RTPCR) for SARS-CoV-2 within 38 days of the second dose. 76 A more recent study by Fazli et al. of 947 individuals suggested that contralateral boosting of the ndLN was associated with detection of higher SARS-CoV-2-spike-binding antibodies, as measured by a bioluminescent assay at later time points after 2–3 weeks. 77 However, this study did not sample pre-boosting antibody levels and the early days 5–7 time points. The Fazli et al. data is nevertheless not inconsistent with the mathematical modeling of our data, which showed faster growth resulting in an earlier peak for the dLN and slower growth resulting in a later peak for the ndLN response. However, there is considerable heterogeneity between all these studies and each has its own limitations. Therefore, it will be necessary to establish a large, prospective, multi-center randomized controlled trial to compare the vaccine efficacy of ipsilateral vs. contralateral boosting to inform future practice. Collectively, these data indicate that boosting of the ipsilateral dLN optimizes the quality and quantity of the recall response early, at a time when herd immunity is urgently needed to short-circuit epidemic outbreaks.

texts.orig: Taken as a whole, these mouse and human data add to the growing field of precision vaccinology as envisioned by Plotkin 78 and identify SSMs and their cell-cell communication with Bmems as potential cellular and molecular targets to improve the depth and breadth of antibody responses and vaccine efficacy.

texts.orig: Limitations of the study
texts.text: Limitations of the study

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We have focused on SSMs but the subcapsular niche is also populated by many other cell types, including marginal reticular cells, lymphatic vascular endothelial cells, and other stromal cells. 23 It will be interesting to determine what role, if any, stromal cell ' 'memory' ' plays in vaccine-induced immunity. Innate-like lymphocytes also localize to the subcapsular niche, 79 and the role of these cells in the Bmem recall response remains to be determined. Although we have focused on single-cell transcriptomics to decode the cellular programming of Bmems, it is likely that epigenetic controls play an important role in their cell fate potential. The human study was designed to obtain correlative data for the early vaccine response. We were restricted by the number of blood collections and could not more precisely model the kinetics of the serum NAb recall response. Similarly, we were unable to perform FNB before antigen recall. In addition, the currently available antibody and BCR database only allowed us to map 71 B cells in our dataset to previously reported SARSCoV-2-specific BCRs. We hope to resolve these issues as our knowledge and datasets expand with future studies.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All experimental procedures with mice were reviewed and approved by the Garvan Institute of Medical Research/St Vincent's Hospital Animal Ethics Committee. All mice were bred and maintained in specific pathogen-free (SPF) animal housing at Australian BioResources and the Garvan Institute of Medical Research Biological Testing Facility. Mice genotyping was performed by the Garvan Molecular Genetics (GMG) facility and all experiments described in this study were performed at the Garvan Biological Testing Facility (BTF). Wild-type C57BL/6J mice (CD45.2 allele) and congenic B6.SJL-Ptprc a Pepc b /BoyJAusb mice (CD45.1 allele) were purchased from Australian BioResources (Moss Vale, Australia). HyHEL10 B cell receptor knock-in (SWHEL) mice have been described previously. 29 These mice carry a single copy of anti-HEL heavy chain (VH10) coding exon targeted to the endogenous Ighb allele plus multiple copies of anti-HEL light chain (V κ 10-κ) variable region genes. These SWHEL mice were maintained on a C57BL/6J (CD45.2 allele) or C57BL/6-SJL.Ptprc a/a (CD45.1 allele) background. TdTomato transgenic mice were generated by crossing floxed tdTomato reporter mice (B6.Cg-Gt(ROSA) 26Sort rtm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze /J) 82 with ROSA26-Cre mice that ubiquitously expresses Cre recombinase (B6.129S4-Gt(ROSA) 26Sort rtm1Sor/ r/J). 83 SW HEL mice were crossed to tdTomato and Blimp-1 Egfp/+ reporter mice, 84 as well as to Kaede transgenic mice (Tg(CAG-Kaede)#Kgwa) 85 to generate tdTomato.Blimp-1 Egfp/+ SW HEL mice and Kaede SW HEL mice respectively. These mice were maintained on a C57BL6/J background. OT-II TCR transgenic mice expressing a TCR with monoclonal specificity against ovalbumin (OVA)-derived peptide have been previously described (B6.Cg-Tg(TcraTcrb425Cbn/J). 86 CFP transgenic mice expressing cyan fluorescent protein under the β–actin promoter (Tg(ACTB-ECFP)1Nagy/J) 87 and Thy1.1 congenic mice were crossed to OT-II mice to generate Cyan OT-II and Thy1.1 OT-II mice and maintained on a C57BL/6J background. Smarta TCR transgenic mice (B6.Cg-Ptprc a Pepc b .Tg(TcrLCMV)1Aox/PpmJ) expressing a TCR that recognizes lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) glycoprotein-derived peptide have been previously described. 88

texts.orig: Following written informed consent, participants were enrolled into the COVAXIR Study (peripheral blood and LN FNB), approved by St. Vincent's Hospital Sydney Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC: 2021/ETH00180) or blood collection only (HREC: 2019/ ETH03336). Information about participant age and sex is available in Table S3 . To ensure study participants had no previous SARS-CoV-2 infection at study enrolment, serum was collected and tested for SARS-CoV-2 IgG 89 on the Abbott Architect SARSCoV-2 IgG assay 90 and EUROIMMUN Anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG ELISA assay. 91 Thirty healthy individuals with no previous SARSCoV-2 infection were recruited between May-August 2021. Participants received the second BNT162b2 vaccine dose either in the same arm (boosted dLN, n = 20) or opposite arm (boosted ndLN, n = 10).

texts.orig: To isolate naı¨ ¨ ¨ve SW HEL B cells and OT-II T cells for adoptive transfer experiments, donor SWHEL and OT-II mice were sacrificed by CO 2 inhalation and cervical dislocation. The spleen, as well as inguinal, axillary, and brachial LNs, were harvested into 2FD media (2% FBS in DMEM). Tissues were mashed through a 70 μm nylon mesh filter on a 50 ml conical tube with a 1 ml syringe plunger, washed with 5 ml of RBC lysis buffer (150 mM NH4Cl, 10 mM KHCO3 , and 0.1 mM Na 2 EDTA), underlaid with 1 ml of FBS, and centrifuged at 1500 rpm, 5 mins, 4 ◦ C. Cells were then washed twice with 10 ml of 2FD and once with 10 ml of MACs buffer (0.5% bovine serum albumin, 2 mM EDTA, and 0.09% NaN3 in PBS) and then resuspended at 10 8 cells/ml. To enrich SW HEL B cells from single cell suspension, non-B cells were depleted by labelling with biotinylated anti-CD4, anti-CD8, anti-CD11b, anti-CD11c, and anti-CD43

texts.orig: monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). To enrich OT-II T cells, non-CD4 + T cells were depleted by labelling with anti-B220, anti-CD11b, antiCD11c, anti-CD8, and anti-Ly6G mAbs. Labelled cell suspensions were washed with 10mL MACS buffer after 30 minutes of incubation on ice, resuspended at 10 8 cells/ml, and magnetically labelled by mixing with anti-biotin microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec) at 1:25 volume ratio. After incubation at 30 minutes on ice, cells were washed and filtered through a 70μm nylon cell strainer and loaded onto LS MACS columns (Miltenyi Biotec) attached to magnetic cell separators. Columns were washed with 2 × 1 ml MACS buffer and total unlabelled cells that pass through the column which contain SWHEL B cells or OT-II T cells were collected. The purity of the isolated donor cells was determined by flow cytometry by staining SWHEL B cells with anti-B220 mAb and two-step staining of HEL and anti-HEL HyHEL9 mAb, while OT-II T cells with anti-CD4 and anti-Vα2 TCR mAbs. Flow cytometry staining procedure is described in detail below. The purity of SWHEL B cells calculated from the proportion of B220 + out of lymphocyte and doublet exclusion gates was typically >98%, while the proportion of HEL-binding SWHEL B cells calculated from the proportion of HEL + B220 + was typically 15%. The purity of OT-II T cells calculated from a proportion of CD4 + Vα2 TCR + out of lymphocyte and doublet exclusion gates was typically 75%. Donor cells were resuspended in 2FD media and 2–2.5 × 10 5 of B220 + HEL-binding SWHEL B cells with an equal number of CD4 + Vα2 + OT-II T cells were injected intravenously through retroorbital route into age and sex-matched 6–10-week-old naı¨ ¨ ¨ve recipient mice. Recipient mice were rested overnight before primary immunisation the next day. Smarta T cells were also prepared similarly to OT-II T cells.

texts.orig: HEL-OVA vaccine was prepared by conjugating HEL protein to OVA-derived peptide 323–339 (CGGISQAVHAAHAEINEAGR) by using cross-linking agent succinimidyl-6-([ß-maleimidopropionamido] hexanoate) (SMPH) (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The addition of non-native cysteine-glycine-glycine (CGG) amino acid residues (underlined above) at the N-terminal of the OVA peptide is critical for SMPH-facilitated HEL-OVA conjugation since SMPH crosslinker works by conjugating primary amines on protein to sulfhydryl-containing molecules such as cysteine. The two glycine residues were added to the peptide for flexibility. 113,114 HEL protein was first resuspended at 2 mg/ml in PBS and mixed with 100 mM DMSO-resuspended SMPH. The HEL-SMPH mixture was incubated at room temperature on rocker for 2 hours and were then dialyzed overnight with either 10 kDa Slide-A-Lyzer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) or 12.4 kDa dialysis tubing (Sigma) against 5 L PBS. The next day the concentration of HEL-SMPH was measured with NanoDrop spectrophotometer and 7× molar excess of 5 mM OVA peptide resuspended in sterile H2O was added. The HELSMPH and OVA peptide mixture was incubated for 4 hours at room temperature on a rocker and dialyzed overnight as described above. The dialyzed HEL-SMPH-OVA (hereafter called HEL-OVA) concentration was measured the next day and run on SDSPAGE to check for successful conjugation indicated by higher molecular weight compared to unconjugated HEL. HEL-OVA was aliquoted at 1 mg/ml and stored at -70 ◦ C for long term or at 4 ◦ C for not more than two months. HEL 3X -OVA was also prepared with the same protocol using HEL 3X protein. HEL-gp61 was prepared by conjugating HEL to LCMV glycoprotein-derived peptide 61–80 (CGGGLKGPDIYKGVYQFKS-VEFD; underlined are non-native CGG residues). Vaccines for immunisation were prepared by mixing HEL-OVA with Sigma Adjuvant System (SAS) (Sigma-Aldrich). SAS was reconstituted with 1 ml sterile PBS and warmed to 37 ◦ C for 30 minutes before mixing with HEL-OVA at equal volume (e.g., 10 μl of SAS with 10 μl of 1 mg/ml HEL-OVA). For primary immunization, recipient mice were immunized subcutaneously with 10 μg adjuvanted HEL-OVA on one side of the lower flank. For secondary immunization, >28 days after primary immunisation mice were reimmunized subcutaneously with 20 μg adjuvanted HEL-OVA either on the same lower flank side or on the other side of the lower flank. HEL 3X -OVA and HEL-gp61 were prepared and administered similarly. For PE immunization, PE (ProZyme RPE, Agilent) at 1 mg/ml was mixed with equal volume of SAS. Mice were subcutaneously primed and boosted with 15 μg and 30 μg of adjuvanted PE, respectively.

texts.orig: Single cell suspensions were aliquoted into 96-well V bottom plates. For LNs, all cells from a single LN were used for staining in a single well. All staining steps were performed in 50 μl PBA except for staining with anti-CD138 mAb which was stained in PBA without NaN 3. This was required because CD138 staining intensity is reduced in the presence of azide. 92 Incubation with antibodies or other staining reagents was performed on ice, protected from light, and with an incubation time for 30–45 mins. Cells were washed 2–3 times between staining steps with the addition of 150 μl PBA and centrifuged at 2100 rpm, 4 ◦ C for 1 min. Typically, cells were first incubated with anti-CD16/CD32 mAb and HEL protein at 200 ng/ml in PBA to block non-specific antibody binding to Fc receptors and to detect HEL binding, respectively. This was followed by staining with a pre-determined optimal dilution of HyHEL9-AF647 mAb and other fluorochrome-conjugated mAb. For HEL 3X binding staining, cells were incubated with anti-CD16/32 mAb and HEL 3X (50 ng/ml), a sub-saturating level for the unmutated SWHEL BCR. This was followed by staining with anti-IgG1 mAb and blocking with 10% normal mouse serum, before staining with HyHEL9-AF647 mAb and other fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies. Blocking with normal mouse serum was required because the HyHEL9 mAb is a BALB/c IgG1 isotype and would otherwise be bound by previously added anti-mouse IgG1 mAb. If staining for CD45.1, CD45.2, and B220, staining steps were separated between anti-CD45.1/ 2 and anti-B220 mAbs to avoid competitive binding. In addition, staining with the streptavidin conjugate was always left to the last staining step to avoid non-specific binding to HEL. Cells were washed 3 times with PBA as above and finally resuspended in 100μl PBA. Single stained control samples were prepared by staining UltraComp eBeads (Invitrogen) with each of the fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies used in each experiment. Unstained cells or beads and no-HEL control sample were also prepared.

texts.orig: Flow cytometry data acquisitions were performed on either LSR II SORP or Fortessa (BD Biosciences). Samples were filtered through 35 μm filter round-bottom tubes (Corning) just prior to data acquisition. Photomultiplier tube (PMT) voltage for each detector was adjusted using single stained control samples before running all samples with the optimal PMT voltage setting. Flow cytometry data were exported and analysed using FlowJo software v10.8. Compensation matrices were automatically generated using acquired single stained controls, manually checked, and applied to all samples. Lymphocytes were identified based on their forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) properties, excluding dead cells and debris. Doublets were excluded by FSC and SSC-height vs -area gates. In adoptive transfer experiments, cells from donor mice were separated from recipient mice cells based either on their fluorescent marker (e.g., Kaede/tdTomato) or on CD45.1/CD45.2 expression depending on the experimental settings. For HEL-binding staining, no-HEL control sample was used to delineate HEL-binding cells in the experimental samples.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Blood was collected from mice by tail nicking or by cardiac puncture (if terminal procedure) into 1.5 ml microcentrifuge tube and centrifuged at 13,300 rpm for 10 minutes to separate the serum. Collected serum samples were stored at -20 ◦ C. All ELISA procedure was performed in 384-well high-binding microplates (Corning). Unless indicated otherwise, each of the incubation steps was for 1 hour and 37 ◦ C followed by the washing step consisting of three washing cycles with ELISA wash buffer (0.05% Tween-20 in PBS) by using a microplate washer (Tecan). ELISA plate was coated in 30 μl/well of 10 μg/ml HEL in NPP buffer (34.9 mM NaHCO3 , 15 mM Na 2 CO 3, 3.1 mM NaN 3, and 1 mM MgCl2) and incubated overnight at 4 ◦ C in the dark. The next day, the plate was washed and blocked with 80 μl of 1% BSA in PBS. Serum samples were serially diluted to 1:50, 1:150, 1:450, 1:1350, and 1:4050 in 0.1% BSA in PBS and were added in duplicate to the wells. Control antibody HyHEL10 IgG1 mAb was also diluted to multiple serial dilutions and added to separate wells to generate a standard curve with known concentration. After incubation and washing steps, HEL-binding antibody was detected with biotinylated anti-Igκ light chain or anti-IgG1 mAb at 1:1000 dilution in 0.1% BSA, and 1% skim milk in PBS. Streptavidin-alkaline phosphatase (Invitrogen) at 1:2000 dilution in 0.1% BSA in PBS was added to the wells. Alkaline phosphatase substrate p-nitrophenyl phosphate (MP Biomedicals) at 1 mg/ml in NPP buffer was finally added to visualize the enzymatic reaction from bound HEL-binding antibody. The absorbance of the reaction was read at 405 nm on a microplate reader (BioTek Instruments). The concentration of anti-HEL antibodies from the serum samples was interpolated from the standard curve using the inverse-variance weighted estimation method implemented in R. 93 For measurement of HEL 3X -binding antibody level, ELISA was done similarly except HEL 3X protein was used for ELISA plate coating at 5 μg/ml in NPP buffer, and HyHEL5 IgG1 mAb was used as antibody control to generate the standard curve.

texts.orig: LNs were fixed in 4% formaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich) overnight at 4 ◦ C and then transferred into 30% sucrose overnight at 4 ◦ C. LNs were then embedded in Tissue-Tek O.C.T. compound (Sakura Finetek) and snap-frozen in cryomolds with liquid nitrogen-cooled isopropanol. Frozen LNs were stored at-80 ◦ C until use. Sections of 7-μm thick were cut using a CM3050S cryostat (Leica), transferred to SuperFrost Plus glass slides (Thermo Scientific), fixed in ice-cold acetone for 8 minutes, and dried overnight at room temperature. For immunofluorescence staining, sections were first blocked with 30% horse serum (Invitrogen) plus 3% BSA in PBS for 30 minutes. Sections were washed with PBS and stained with anti-CD169 and anti-GFP antibodies in a humidified chamber for 1 hour at room temperature in the dark. The stained sections were washed and mounted in Fluoromount-G (Southern Biotech) and imaged with Leica DM5500 microscope. The acquired images were processed with Adobe Photoshop. Imaris v9.8 (Oxford Instruments) software was used to quantify fluorescence intensity of cells of interest using the spot detection function.

texts.orig: Mouse was anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of a mixture of ketamine and xylazine at 100 mg and 10 mg per kg body weight, respectively. To maintain anesthesia, 1− 2% isoflurane in 100% oxygen at a flow rate of 500 ml/min was used via a nose cone. Mouse was kept at 37 ◦ C during the whole procedure on a customized heated SmartStage (Biotherm). Lacri-Lube was applied to mouse eyes to prevent drying out. The right flank and inguinal area were shaved with electric hair clippers, and the remaining hair was removed using micropore tape before sterilizing the skin with ethanol swabs. Sterile spring microdissection scissors was used to make an incision on the abdominal skin along the midline and right hind leg, and a skin flap exposing the inguinal LN was made separated from the abdominal muscle. PDMS polymer (Dow Corning) was used as a base stuck to the heating pad by thermal conductive T-putty (LairdTech). Skin flap was immobilized on PDMS base by gluing the edges with VetBond tissue adhesive (3M) with the inguinal LN positioned in the middle. The location of the inguinal LN was determined, and the cortical side was exposed by carefully removing overlaying skin as well as fat and fascia layers with microdissection scissors and microforceps. PBS/saline was continuously applied to make sure LN stays moist. A small O-ring (washer) was placed with silicone grease over the skin flap, surrounding the exposed inguinal LN. The space inside the O-ring was filled with saline and/or Immersol (Carl Zeiss) over the inguinal LN to create a meniscus.

texts.orig: For explant LN imaging, mouse was sacrificed by CO2 inhalation and cervical dislocation to harvest inguinal LN into PBS. Fat and connective tissues were carefully removed from the LN under a stereomicroscope with low-level illumination. LN was mounted on its medullary side on a plastic coverslip with VetBond tissue glue. Excess tissue glue was removed to prevent autofluorescent. Silicone grease was used to stick the coverslip to a small petri dish, and the LN was then immersed in PBS for imaging.

texts.orig: Intravital imaging was performed on a Zeiss 7MP two-photon microscope (Carl Zeiss) equipped with a Chameleon Vision II ultrafast Ti:Sa laser (Coherent Scientific). A W Plan-Apochromat 20×/1.0 DIC (UV) Vis-IR water immersion objective lens was used. Excitation wavelengths used were 890–920 nm, and fluorescent images were acquired using non-descanned detectors SP 485 (SHG and CFP), BP 500–550 (Kaede, GFP, and CFP), BP 565–610 (Kaede red and tdTomato) and BP 640–710 (Alexa Fluor 680 and CF680). Typically for time-lapse movie acquisition, a series of planes of 3 μm z-stack spanning a depth of 150–300 μm at an xy resolution of 512 × 512 pixel (425.1 × 425.1 μm) were acquired every 30–45 s. For acquiring static image of whole LN, 5 × 6 tiles were acquired with a series of 3 μm z-stack of 200–450 μm at an xy resolution of 512 × 512 pixel (425 × 425 μm).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Image processing and analyses were done using Imaris v9.8 (Oxford Instruments). Raw image files were imported into the Imaris, and image intensities and thresholds were adjusted with a Gaussian filter used to optimize signal-to-noise ratio. To correct for motion artefacts in time-lapse movie, non-motile SSMs were detected by the spot detection function and drift correction function was applied to the whole dataset. To detect and identify cells, the Imaris spot detection function was used, and the cellular motion was tracked semiautomatically by using the Imaris tracking function aided by manual corrections. SSM layer was identified based on CD169 labelling by using the Imaris surface function. Individual tracks (fortime-lapse movie) or spots (for whole LN) were identified to be inside SSM layerif they have nearest distance ≤0 μm to SSM-rendered surface. Only cells that can be tracked for at least 10 minutes were used for analysis. For SSM depletion experiments (Figure 2), to obtain comparable analysis between control and anti-CSF1R-treated dLNs, capsule layer from the second harmonic generation (SHG) was used as a proxy for the subcapsular sinus region because anti-CSF1R-treated dLNs lacked SSM layer. Cell track spatiotemporal position data were exported from the Imaris Statistics function, including speed, displacement, track length, meandering index, nearest distance to SSM rendered surface, as well as XYZ coordinate. Mean square displacements (MSD) of pooled data were calculated from the exported XYZ coordinates by using CellTrackR. 94 Slope α was calculated using a linear regression from log-transformed data. Slope α=1 indicates Brownian motion of randomly moving cells; α>1 indicates superdiffusive motility; and α<1 indicates subdiffusive motility. 95 Motility coefficient (M) is a measure of the average area a cell scans and was calculated from the slope of the regression line as M=x2 x2 /6t , where x is the displacement at time t . 96

texts.orig: Collection and preparation of human LN samples
texts.text: Collection and preparation of human LN samples

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ultrasound guided FNBs (sometimes referred to as fine needle aspiration biopsy, FNAB) were performed on 18 participants at the Medical Imaging Department of St. Vincent's Hospital Sydney Australia, as previously described. 42 , 97 Following identification of a suitable LN via ultrasound and local anaesthetic, the target LN was sampled via four separate passes of a 25-gauge needle, collecting LN cells by capillary action. Each needle was flushed into a 15mL tube (Falcon, Becton Dickinson [BD], NJ, USA) with 10mL Roswell Park Memorial Institute [RPMI-1640; Gibco, Life Technologies, CA, USA] supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated 0.2 μm syringefiltered foetal calf serum (FCS; Gibco, Life Technologies). The LN samples were used fresh to avoid cell loss during cryopreservation. Peripheral blood collected into serum separating tubes (SST) were centrifuged at 1000×g for 10 minutes. The separated serum was aliquoted and stored at -80 ◦ C until use. LN samples were collected at day 5-7 post-boosting and peripheral blood samples were collected for the day 5-7 (range: 5-9 days, median: 6 days), 4 weeks (range: 21-88 days, median: 29 days) and 4-6 months (range: 122-195 days, median: 170 days) post-boosting study timepoints.

texts.text: Live-cell flow cytometry assay

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A live-cell flow cytometry assay was used to detect the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine-induced IgG antibodies. 50 , 51 Individual SARS-CoV-2 full-length Spike Wuhan-1 D614, Membrane and Envelope proteins were transiently expressed on transfected HEK293 cells. Serum (n = 18) was diluted 1:80 and added to the cells before staining with IgG-AF647 (H+L) (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The LSRII flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) was then used to acquire the cells. Samples were positive for SAR-CoV-2 vaccine antibodies if at least two of the three quality-controlled experiments resulted in a higher median fluorescence intensity (DMFI LJ = LJ MFI transfected cells – MFI non-transfected cells) than the positive threshold (mean DMFI + 4SD of 24 pre-pandemic controls). Post-flow analysis was performed on FlowJo 10.4.1 (TreeStar, USA), Excel (Microsoft, USA), and GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, USA).

texts.orig: Live virus neutralizing antibody assay
texts.text: Live virus neutralizing antibody assay

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The NAb assay was performed as previously described. 54 Clonal HAT-24 cells were generated by transducing lentiviral particles into HEK292T (Thermo Fisher, R70007) cells to stably express ACE2 and TMPRSS2 receptors. These were then trypsinized and resuspended in DMEM-5% foetal bovine serum (FBS) and stained with Hoechst-33342 (5% v/v) live nuclear dye (Invitrogen, R37605) and seeded in a 384-well plate at 1.6 × 10 4 cells per well. Participant sera (n = 30) was serially diluted (2-fold) with DMEM-5% FBS and an equal volume of SARS-CoV-2 virus solution at 2x the median lethal dose (2x LD50) was added to the diluted sera. SARS-CoV-2 variants used were ancestral Clade A.2.2 (D614), Delta (B.1.617.2), and Omicron-BA.1; -BA.2; -BA.5. Sera-virus mixture was incubated for 1hr at 37 ◦ C before 40 μl per well was added to the plated cells. Plates were incubated for 20 hours at 37 ◦ C, 5% CO2 before enumerating nuclear counts with high-content fluorescence microscopy using Cytiva InCell Analyzer HS2500 and IN Carta software. Percentage of virus neutralisation was calculated with the formula %N = (D-(1-Q)) x 100/D (where Q=nuclei count / average count for uninfected controls, and D=1-Q = average count for infected controls). Sigmoidal dose-response curves and interpolated IC50 values (reciprocal dilution at which 50% neutralization is achieved) were determined using Sigmoidal, 4PL model of regression analysis in GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, USA). For assigning of WHO IU, the WHO standard NIBSC code 21/338 was tested against a 10% IVIG preparation (Privigen Batch# P100375874; 28/9/2021) 53 where WHO IU were assigned to this IVIG batch following three independent validations. All subsequent tests were then performed throughout using the above IVIG batch with determined WHO IU/ml. Given the divergence of Omicron lineages and the fact they were not tested within the WHO serology standard validation, we then followed the initial WHO guidelines which recommended using the same unitage for each variant. To establish this, we tested the Ancestral (herein Clade A.2.2) isolate using our above 10% IVIG control with known WHO units in every neutralization assay, and this established the WHO IU per run. For calculations of variant WHO IU, we calculate as this as follows: [IC50 value for serum sample for a variant]/[IC50 value for 10% IVIG tested against Ancestral A.2.2] x the assigned WHO IU (7670 IU/ml) for that 10% IVIG preparation. The lowest dilution used was a 1:20 dilution. The assays were performed in two separate runs, therefore when converting to WHO IU, calculations were performed using the IC50 value for 10% IVIG tested against Ancestral A.2.2 on each specific run, resulting in minor differences in the limit of detection (LOD) in WHO units for each run. Calculated LODs were 31.2 and 26.6 WHO IU for runs 1 and 2 respectively. The LOD used in subsequent analysis was the geometric mean of these LODs, being 28.8.

texts.orig: We fit the models using a mixed effects technique, which means that each parameter has an estimated mean value (fixed effect), and for each subject, parameters are taken from a normal distribution with a mean of the fixed effect and a fitted standard deviation across all subjects (random effect). A diagonal random effect structure was used, which assumes there is no correlation within the random effects. The model was fitted to the log-transformed NAb titres. A constant error residual model was used in the model fitting, assuming the error follows a normal distribution with zero mean and an unknown standard deviation, δ (where δ is estimated in the fitting procedure). A mixed-effect regression method that allows for censoring at the limit of detection was used to estimate the parameters in the model. Model fitting was performed using Monolix2023R1 (LIXOFT) using the lixoftconnector package in R (v3.3.0).

All NAb titres for the variant were then divided by this scaling factor to obtain the scaled NAb titres. Scaled NAb titres were sampled from a normal distribution with a mean of the scaled NAb titres in the relevant arm at the relevant time point and a standard deviation given by the standard error in the scaled NAb titres in the relevant arm at the relevant time point. texts.orig: The following fluorescently conjugated monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) were used to perform immunophenotyping: CD45AlexaFluor700, CD20-APC-Cy7, CD3-PERCP-Cy5.5, IgD-BV421, CD19-BV786, CD27-PE-CF594, and CD38-PE-Cy7. Following collection, the LN samples (n = 16) were pelleted in a centrifuge at 335 ×g for 7 mins at 25 ◦ C and resuspended in residual media. To block Fc receptors, 5 μl of Human TruStain FcX per million cells was added in 100 μl staining volume at room temperature (RT) for 15 mins in the dark. The cocktail of surface mAbs was added into each sample tube, vortexed and incubated at RT in the dark for 15 mins. To remove possible red blood cell (RBC) contamination, 2 ml FACS Lyse was added for 10 mins, samples were washed by centrifuge with Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline (DPBS) at 335 ×g for 7 mins. Supernatant was discarded and the Human FoxP3 Buffer Set (BD Pharmingen) was used for intracellular and intranuclear staining. Samples were incubated with Buffer A (made according to the manufacturer's instructions) for 10 mins at RT in the dark, then washed with 2 ml DPBS supplemented with 0.5 g bovine serum albumin (Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.1 g sodium azide (Sigma-Aldrich) (PBA) by centrifugation at 456 ×g for 7 mins. Supernatant was discarded and cell suspension was incubated for 30 mins at RT in the dark with Buffer C (made according to manufacturer's instructions). Sample was then washed again at 456 ×g for 7 mins with 2 ml PBA and stained with the intracellular and intranuclear mAbs for 30 mins at RT in the dark. A final wash at 456 ×g for 7 mins, then the supernatant was discarded, and the stained cells fixed with 100 μl 0.5% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Samples were acquired on a BD LSRFortessa SORP Analyzer and analysed on FlowJo version 10.8.2 (BD).

texts.orig: Single-cell suspensions were prepared from harvested tissue using enzymatic digestion as described above. Cells were first incubated with Fc receptor blockers anti-CD16/CD32 mAb and labelled with HEL at 200 ng/ml in PBA, after which cells were washed three times with PBA. Cells were then stained with anti-B220 BV786, anti-CD4 PE-Cy7, anti-Vα2 TCR FITC, anti-Vβ5.1/5.2 TCR PerCP-Cy5.5 mAbs, as well as TotalSeq-A (anti-CD19, CD38, CCR6, CD4, CD45.1, CD45.2) and hashtag oligonucleotide antibodies. Cells from different organs/conditions were stained with different TotalSeq-A hashtag antibodies: dLN (hashtag 1), ndLN (hashtag 2), spleen (hashtag 3), naı¨ ¨ ¨ve LN (hashtag 4), and naı¨ ¨ ¨ve spleen (hashtag 6). After staining with mAbs, cells were washed three times with PBA and finally resuspended in 500μl PBA. DAPI was added to each sample just before sorting at a final concentration 0.1 μg/ml. HEL-binding B cells and Vα2 + Vβ5.1/2 + cells were sorted into RPMI 1640 with 10% FBS. After sorting, cells were combined to run on 10x Genomics platform. The Garvan-Weizmann Centre for Cellular Genomics (GWCCG) performed the single-cell capture, library preparation, and sequencing as an in-house commercial service, using the Chromium Single-Cell v2 3' Kits (10x Genomics). The libraries were sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (NovaSeq Control Software v1.7.0 / Real Time Analysis v3.4.4) using NovaSeq S2 130 cycles kit (Illumina, 20497313 as follows: 28 bp (Read 1), 91 bp (Read 2) and 8 bp (Index)). The sequencing of the libraries was performed by the Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics.

texts.orig: For gene expression library, the binary base call (BCL) raw data from the sequencer were demultiplexed and converted to FASTQ format using Cell Ranger v6.0.1 (10x Genomics) mkfastq pipeline. For antibody-derived tag (ADT) and hashtag libraries, Illumina Conversion Software bcl2fastq was used to convert BCL file to FASTQ format. The Cell Ranger multi pipeline was used for alignment, filtering, barcode counting, and unique molecular identifier (UMI) counting from FASTQ files against mouse reference genome mm102020-A. The sequence of fluorescence reporters Tdtomato (tdTomato CDS-WPRE-bGH poly(A) signal) and cyan fluorescence protein (Cfp) genes were incorporated into the reference genome using Cell Ranger mkref to allow distinguish tdTomato-SWHEL B cells and cyan OT-II T cells from recipient mice cells. Intronic mapped reads were also included in Cell Ranger multi pipeline. The pipeline was executed on a high-performance cluster with a Linux 4.15.0-143-generic operating system.

texts.orig: Gene expression and feature barcode (ADT and hashtag) count matrix from Cell Ranger output were used as input for further analyses with Seurat (v4.1.1) using R (v.4.1.0). 101 Cells with more than 1500 genes were considered doublets and were filtered out as well as cells with more than 10% of UMIs mapped to mitochondrial genes. Hash-tagged cells were demultiplexed using HTODemux function, and cells classified as doublet were removed. SCTransform function was used to normalize the dataset including the percent of mitochondria expression as regression factor. Principal components analysis (PCA) was performed using the normalized, mean-centered, and scaled SCT dataset (RunPCA function). Two-dimensional projections were generated using the top 30 PCA vectors as input to RunUMAP function in Seurat. Cells were clustered using the FindNeighbors (top 30 PCA vectors) and FindClusters functions (resolutions 0.8). ADT counts were normalized with centered log ratio transformation (CLR in NormalizeData function). After initial filtering, normalisation, and clustering, expression of ADT-CD45.1, ADT-CD45.2, ADT-CD19, and ADT-CD4, as well as tdTomato and CFP genes were used to classify cells as donor-derived B cells (CD19 + CD4 − CD45.2 + CD45.1 − tdTomato +/ − ), recipientderived B cells (CD19 + CD4 − CD45.1 + CD45.2 − tdTomato − ), donor-derived T cells (CD4 + CD19 − CD45.2 + CD45.1 − Cfp +/ − ), or recipient-derived T cells (CD4 + CD19 − CD45.1 + CD45.2 − Cfp − ) aided by CellSelector and plots from FeatureScatter functions. Ambiguous cells (e.g., cells that were Cfp + CD19 + or Tdtomato + CD4 + ) were removed from analysis. All B cells were further subsetted and the entire scRNA-seq processing pipeline above was re-run using B cells only. Imputation was performed using Adaptively thresholded Low-Rank Approximation (ALRA) to account for dropout during differential gene expression analysis. 115 Differentially expressed genes between different clusters or organs/conditions were identified using the FindAllMarkers function using default settings (Wilcoxon test and Bonferroni P-value correction). HEL + recipient-derived B cells that were also sorted and captured were excluded from downstream analysis because the number of cells that passed the quality control above was too small.

texts.orig: To perform ligand-receptor pair analysis using NicheNet 41 we first defined Bmem from the dLN or ndLN as the receiving cell population. We then used differentially upregulated genes in dLN or ndLN Bmems as our gene set of interest, and all other expressed genes in the receiving cells served as the background gene set. As potential ligand-producing cells, we obtained single-cell data of SSM from Grootveld, Kyaw et al. 33 and performed integration with Seurat, producing a singular dataset that contained dLN Bmems, ndLN Bmems, and SSMs. We then identified all ligands (as defined by NicheNet's curated model) that were expressed in at least 10% of SSMs. We further filtered these ligands to include only those in which the corresponding receptors were expressed in at least 10% of the receiving Bmems. NicheNet was then used to rank each potential ligand according to how well its predicted regulatory potential explained membership in the gene set of interest compared with the background genes, quantified by the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR). Top-ranked ligands were selected, and their predicted target genes and corresponding receptors were visualized in heatmaps and Circos plots to highlight putative ligand–receptor interactions

texts.orig: 15 nearest neighbours (k) in scran's buildSNNGraph were generated, with a total of 15 clusters identified via the igraph 106 cluster_ louvain function. Potential doublet cells were removed if identified by 3 doublet-finding algorithms and replicate runs: 'scDblFinder' 107 (threshold >= 0.85 across ten runs); 'singleCellTK's' runDoubletFinder 108 (threshold >= 0.63 across three runs); and 'single cell doublet scoring' (sdcs)'s binary classification doublet scoring (bcds) 109 (threshold >= 0.81 across two runs). Additional doublets, identified by dual cell-type features, were also removed. Unsupervised UMAP and SNNG clustering of the filtered data was undertaken using ten dimensions and eighteen k nearest neighbours, with a total of 14 clusters identified. B cell clusters, identified by high expression of MS4A1 , low expression of CD3E/G , and a high proportion of cells with BCR, were then subset into a new SingleCellExperiment object for B cell gene expression analysis. Additional filtering was undertaken to remove cells expressing CD3E or CD3G and cells not expressing either MS4A1 or CD19 , resulting in 24,211 B cells. To achieve greater resolution within the B cell populations, the ribosomal and IGKV and IGLV genes were removed from the GEX analysis, the top 2000 HVGs were found, and these were used to re-integrate the data subset by the 10X capture date. Clustering and SNNG was run using 15 dimensions and nearest neighbours k=18. To understand the DEGs between the clusters, scran's findMarkers function was used with the logfold-change threshold set to 0.5.

texts.orig: For the BCR analysis, only cells that passed the gene expression analysis pipeline were considered for subsequent BCR analysis. Cells were also omitted from subsequent BCR analysis on the basis of non-productive rearrangements, unidentified V or J gene usage, and more than one productive heavy or light chain. The full-length consensus BCR sequences assembled by Cell Ranger were further aligned using IMGT/HighV-QUEST 80 to determine the IGH V gene mutations. B cell clones, involving paired heavy and light chains, assessed across both samples per study participant, were identified using agglomerative clustering with a distance threshold of 0.15 (length scaled Levenshtein distance) between pairs of CDR3 nucleotide sequences from BCRs with matching V and J genes (Sci-kit-learn Python library version 1.2.2). BCR clones were mapped to previously reported SARS-CoV-2-specific BCR or Ab sequences 81 , 110 , 111 based on matching V and J genes and at least 85% identity of the CDR3 amino acid sequence for the heavy chain of at least one of the cells associated with the clone. For identifying V and J gene matches for both assessing clonality and mapping to previously reported SARS-CoV-2-specific BCR sequences, some V and J genes for which a high frequency of multiple best-matched genes were observed were grouped. BCR diversity was assessed using the Shannon diversity index. 112

For identifying V and J gene matches for both assessing clonality and mapping to previously reported SARS-CoV-2-specific BCR sequences, some V and J genes for which a high frequency of multiple best-matched genes were observed were grouped. BCR diversity was assessed using the Shannon diversity index. 112

Unless otherwise stated, statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism v9. Quantitative data differences between two groups were compared by unpaired Student t test for normally distributed data or by Mann-Whitney test for non-Gaussian distributed data unless otherwise specified. Data distribution normality were analysed by using D'Agostino-Pearson test or by Shapiro-Wilk normality test for small sample number (n≤4). Significant differences were determined by two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test for multiple comparisons. When comparing NAb results between human vaccine groups, the Mann-Whitney test for multiple comparisons with Holm-Sı 
´ � ´ da´ ´ k method was used. P-values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
